scenes.tts: A whole nerve is a tangle of many fibres. So no one could say what one sensory ending sent to the brain. What does one neuron do, in time, when a stimulus, movement or reward changes? Recording from inside a cell answers that, but only for a cell you can impale. This method asks it from outside, in intact tissue.
scenes.visual: A nerve of many fibres between a sensory ending and the brain, one fibre marked with a question; then stimulus, movement and reward feeding one neuron with a question about its firing; then an electrode inside one cell versus outside a cell in tissue.
scenes.narration: A whole nerve is a tangle of many fibres. So no one could say what one sensory ending sent to the brain. What does one neuron do, in time, when a stimulus, movement or reward changes? Recording from inside a cell answers that, but only for a cell you can impale. This method asks it from outside, in intact tissue.

scenes.tts: Active neurons produce currents across their membranes that can be measured in the fluid outside. So a fine electrode placed near a neuron records its action potentials without entering the cell. Hubel and Wiesel used sharpened tungsten wire, insulated with lacquer. In a conscious person, a tungsten needle goes through the skin into a nerve and is moved by hand until the activity of interest is isolated.
scenes.visual: A neuron with current arrows and an electrode beside it; its action potentials appear as brief blips on a trace; then a needle goes through skin into a human nerve, moved by hand until clean blips appear.
scenes.narration: Active neurons produce currents across their membranes that can be measured in the fluid outside. In a conscious person, a tungsten needle goes through the skin into a nerve and is moved by hand until the activity of interest is isolated.

scenes.tts: Spikes from one cell have a characteristic shape. So spikes can be grouped by waveform into units. This step is called spike sorting: decoding the spike times of the recorded neurons from the raw data. In a Purkinje cell, simple and complex spikes differ in shape, so one record gives both.
scenes.visual: A raw trace with spikes of three shapes; spikes are coloured and grouped by shape into three units, each with its own row of ticks; then a Purkinje cell trace with two spike shapes.
scenes.narration: Spikes from one cell have a characteristic shape. So spikes can be grouped by waveform into units. scenes.tts: Stimuli or events are repeated many times, and spikes are aligned to them. Each repeat is one row of a raster, with one tick for each spike. A peristimulus time histogram stacks the repeats, aligned to stimulus onset. It divides each bin's spike count by the number of repeats times the bin width, giving spikes per second.
scenes.visual: Trial rows build one at a time into a raster aligned at stimulus onset; histogram bars grow beneath; the rate formula is shown.
scenes.narration: Stimuli or events are repeated many times, and spikes are aligned to them. Each repeat is one row of a raster, with one tick for each spike. scenes.tts: A tuning curve plots the mean rate against one stimulus value, such as bar orientation, with many trials per value. It is compared with the spontaneous rate. In this idealised cell, a bar at ninety degrees gives forty spikes a second. At thirty and a hundred and fifty degrees, only five to six. With no bar, two.
scenes.visual: Axes of rate against bar orientation; dots at tested orientations; a dashed spontaneous level; the idealised curve with its three marked values, tagged as idealised.

scenes.tts: The method samples only a fraction of cells, and favours large, active cells. In one hippocampal estimate, a tetrode could record signals from about a thousand neurons. Only sixty to a hundred should be detectable, and about six units were usually found. The control is to pair it with imaging, which does not need spikes to be large. A unit may also hold spikes from two neurons. Because a neuron has a refractory period, spikes too close together signal contamination.
scenes.visual: Electrode among cells: only the large active ones are picked up; a funnel from about a thousand to sixty to a hundred to about six; then a row of ticks with two spikes too close together circled.

scenes.tts: Hubel and Wiesel recorded single cells in cat in 1962, and in monkey in 1968. Mapped with moving bars, cat cells fell into simple and complex classes, and monkey cells into simple, complex and hypercomplex, with orientation selectivity. In 1971, O'Keefe and Dostrovsky recorded single units in a freely moving rat's hippocampus. Some cells fired when the animal was at particular places.
scenes.visual: Two panels: a bar rotating before a cell whose ticks burst at its preferred orientation; a dot moving in an arena with spikes only inside one patch.

scenes.tts: In 1994, Mirenowicz and Schultz found that three quarters of recorded monkey dopamine neurons fired to unpredicted liquid. Once a cue predicted it, the response moved to the cue. In 1979, Johansson and Vallbo grouped 334 units from the human median nerve into four classes by firing and receptive field. Keep this rule: a recording shows firing goes with an event, never that firing causes it.
scenes.visual: Rows of ticks showing the burst move from reward to cue; a needle in a nerve with 334 units sorted into four class chips; then the rule in a box.
